segments.title: When cost efficiency works: easily replaced commercial assets
segments.body: Government definitions of efficiency increasingly emphasise cost efficiency, or bang for your buck, over capability efficiency. A focus on cost makes sense when doing without a better option has little consequence or a substitute is easy to find. Standard commercial lorries illustrate why this can be a sensible approach for a company. If an unexpected need arises, the company can hire another lorry.

evidence.note: Government emphasis on cost efficiency and the conditions that make it sensible, illustrated by hiring a standard lorry when circumstances change.

segments.summary: Standard commercial lorries show why cost efficiency can work when an acceptable replacement is easy to obtain.

segments.title: Why military capabilities cannot be hired at short notice
segments.body: A force with only enough fighters, destroyers, and aircraft carriers for the expected demands depends on everything going according to plan. Extra military assets cannot simply be hired when circumstances change. An imagined rental-company call on behalf of the Ministry of Defence asks for fighter squadrons and a destroyer or two, exposing the problem with that assumption. Even if the equipment could be hired, crews would still have to be found. Those crews would need training to operate within the receiving country's systems, so access to equipment alone would leave a further capability gap.

evidence.note: Force levels that depend on everything going to plan, the imagined hire of fighters and destroyers, and the need for crews trained to operate within national systems.

segments.summary: Fighters, destroyers, and aircraft carriers cannot simply be hired to cover a shortfall, and even hired equipment would need suitably trained crews.

segments.title: Why the 1930s Royal Navy preferred more usable submarines
segments.body: Royal Navy planners in the 1930s used capability efficiency to ask whether enough units would exist to guarantee a capability when needed. One objection to very large submarines with big guns was their massive crew requirement. The same manpower could crew three ordinary submarines, which could also be obtained for the cost of one large boat. In the Navy's view, those ordinary boats were nearly as effective as the oversized submarines. The illustrative choice is between three 80-percent solutions and one 95-percent solution, with a clear preference for the three boats.

evidence.note: Royal Navy usage in the 1930s, the crew and cost comparison between one large submarine and three ordinary boats, and the illustrative preference for three 80-percent solutions over one 95-percent solution.

segments.summary: For the crew and cost of one large submarine, three ordinary boats offered the Royal Navy more units that were each nearly as effective in its judgment.

segments.title: Cost efficiency and capability efficiency both have a place
segments.body: Cost efficiency has increasingly become the default measure of efficiency. It works much of the time, so cost remains a useful consideration. The recommendation is to use capability efficiency alongside it instead of treating cost as the best guide in every case.

evidence.note: The recommendation to retain cost efficiency where it works while also using capability efficiency.

segments.summary: Cost efficiency works much of the time, while capability efficiency remains necessary alongside it.
